title: ashes, and forty days
hook: a smudge on the forehead, fish on Friday: giving something up is a way of paying attention

segments.voice: Yesterday: the saints, honored, not worshiped. Today, the one day a year Catholics walk around with a smudge on their foreheads.

One Wednesday a year, a coworker shows up with a black smudge on her forehead. Then the barista. Then a kid on the train. Somebody leans over to say: you've got something on your face. It's Ash Wednesday, and it starts a season. For the next forty days, a Catholic friend might be off chocolate, or off social media, or eating fish on Fridays. It can look like a diet. It isn't about the chocolate.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `IT'S ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT THE CHOCOLATE.`

segments.voice: Lent is the season of forty days before Easter. Forty is the number the Bible keeps reaching for when someone is being tested: Noah's rain, Moses on the mountain, and Jesus fasting in the desert for forty days before he begins his work. Lent walks alongside those forty days. It opens with ash. A cross is traced on the forehead, often with words from the Bible's first pages, in the Douay-Rheims: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim. Catholics hear it as honest: you won't be here forever, so what will you do with the time? Then come three old practices: prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and skip meat on the Fridays of Lent, because Friday is the day Jesus died. The rule doesn't count fish as meat. Hello, Friday fish fry. Many also give something up. Here's the idea underneath: give up something small, and every reach for it becomes a moment of noticing. The empty space where the chocolate was becomes a little room for prayer, or for someone else. And the forty days only make sense because of where they end: Easter morning.
screen: `FORTY: NOAH, MOSES, THE DESERT.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `THE REACH BECOMES A REMINDER.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of one small thing you reach for without thinking: your phone, a snack, a complaint. Picture yourself reaching for it and stopping, hand in the air. Stay in that pause for three slow breaths, and see what you notice there instead.
Lent. Forty days before Easter, of prayer, fasting and giving, where less becomes a way of paying attention. Sixth word.
Your line: less, on purpose. The ash says the time is short; the empty space makes room. Day six, done.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THINGS YOUR FAMILY KEPT.`

original.note: Latin: the fortieth. the Church's Latin name for Lent, still behind Spanish cuaresma and Italian quaresima.

trapdoor: what you thought: six weeks of giving up chocolate.
what it means: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, where less becomes a way of paying attention.
what a scholar hears: Quadragesima, the fortieth; English Lent from Old English lencten, spring; Sundays are not counted in the forty.

story.title: forty days in the desert
story.text: Jesus walks out into the desert and eats nothing for forty days. At the end, starving, he's offered a shortcut: if you're the Son of God, turn these stones into bread. He refuses: a person doesn't live by bread alone. Then he's offered a stunt from the top of the Temple, then every kingdom on earth. He turns down all three, and only then does his work begin.

wrong.myth: Lent is mostly about giving up chocolate.
wrong.truth: it's forty days of prayer, fasting and giving. what you give up is a way of paying attention.

Fasting and abstinence summarized for the Latin Church (ages and local rules vary; in the US, abstinence on the Fridays of Lent). 'The rule doesn't count fish as meat' (canon 1251 speaks of meat; fish is traditionally permitted). Confirm.
'Because Friday is the day Jesus died' (CCC 1438; canon 1250 names Fridays as penitential days). Confirm.
